newsitem.title: USA: Shelton leading candidate for top US military job.
newsitem.headline: Shelton leading candidate for top US military job.

text.p: Army Gen. Henry Shelton, head of the U.S. military's Special Operations Command, has become the leading candidate to be nominated by President Bill Clinton as new chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, defence officials said on Tuesday.

But the officials, who asked not to be identified, declined to confirm a CBS television report that Defence Secretary William Cohen had already decided to recommend that Clinton nominate the square-jawed Shelton for Senate confirmation.
"He is certainly now at the top of the list," one official told Reuters. "But I cannot confirm whether he has been recommended."

Another senior defence official said Cohen had not had a final meeting with Clinton on the choice for a successor to Army Gen. John Shalikashvili, whose term as the nation's top military officer expires at the end of September.
Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters earlier on Tuesday that he expected Clinton to make a decision "in the next several days."
White House spokesman Mike McCurry also said he expected a nomination soon.

Cohen's first choice to replace him, Air Force Gen. Joseph Ralston, withdrew from consideration last month after disclosure of an adulterous affair more than 10 years ago. Ralston is vice chairman of the joint chiefs.

Shelton, 55, is a tall paratrooper who heads the U.S. Special Operations Command based at MacDill Air Force Base in Tampa, Florida. He is a 34-year military veteran and a native of Tarboro, North Carolina.
Shelton, who was commander of the U.S. military operation in Haiti three years ago, is known as a quiet officer who commands great respect and loyalty from his troops.
He served for two years as head of the elite 82nd Airborne Division and also held senior operations posts with the Joint Chiefs of Staff at the Pentagon.
He and other officers in elite special forces units, trained for operations ranging from fighting behind enemy lines to peacekeeping, are known as "snake eaters."

Others believed to be high on Cohen's short list included Marine Corps Commandant Gen. Charles Krulak; Navy Adm. Joseph Lopez, chief of southern NATO forces based in Naples, Italy, and Army Gen. Wesley Clark, recently approved as head of all allied NATO forces in Europe.
Cohen said last week he had narrowed his list of candidates to three or four and had discussed them with Clinton at the NATO summit meeting in Madrid.
He also told reporters flying home with him from Europe on Monday that he planned to hold a final meeting with Clinton on the matter within days.
Defence officials were reluctant to make a prediction after the embarrassing Ralston incident. But several said they believed Shelton was a top candidate.

"Shelton is the kind of guy who the president likes. Both Shelton and Lopez are team players, very capable and with key joint operations experience" involving all military services, said one official privately.
Cohen told reporters who travelled with him to Brussels in mid-June that he would not insist on "abolute perfection" in his search for a new commander despite the Ralston incident.
"I will look for the best possible individual ... a very high standard will be exacted," he said, adding that joint operations experience would be one major factor.
